mcqs.question: Two teams each ship a plain `.card` class with different padding, both loaded on the same page. What actually decides which padding wins?
options: Whichever team's file is alphabetically first in the build
CSS automatically merges the two rules, keeping the larger padding value
The rule appearing later in load/source order wins, purely by accident of import sequence, not by design
Neither applies, and the browser falls back to the default padding
mcqs.explanation: Since both selectors have identical specificity, the cascade's source-order tiebreaker decides — whichever rule was declared later wins, an accident of import order rather than either team's intent. CSS never merges competing values for the same property, and there's no alphabetical rule in the cascade.

mcqs.question: What does BEM actually prevent, and what does it not prevent?
options: It prevents any class name collision entirely, because the build tool rejects duplicate names
It prevents collisions between two components that both follow the naming convention consistently, but doesn't stop someone from writing an unprefixed class name that breaks the pattern
It prevents specificity conflicts by making every class an ID selector
It prevents runtime style recalculation on every render
mcqs.explanation: BEM is a naming convention, not enforced tooling — following it consistently makes collisions unlikely, but nothing at build time stops a developer from writing a bare .card that ignores the pattern. There's no build-tool rejection mechanism, BEM classes stay regular classes rather than IDs, and it has nothing to do with render-time recalculation.

mcqs.question: Why can two different files both define a `.card` class under CSS Modules without any risk of collision?
options: The build tool rewrites each file's class name into a unique generated string before it reaches the browser, so the two never share a runtime class name at all
CSS Modules automatically wrap every stylesheet in a shadow DOM boundary
The bundler deletes one of the two .card definitions during the build
CSS Modules require every class name to include the file path manually
mcqs.explanation: CSS Modules make collisions structurally impossible by having the build step generate a unique class name per source file, so .card in one module and .card in another become two entirely different runtime strings. There's no shadow DOM involved, nothing is deleted, and developers don't manually embed file paths — the tooling does that automatically.

mcqs.question: What real capability does classic CSS-in-JS provide that CSS Modules and BEM don't offer as directly?
options: Zero runtime cost compared to plain CSS
Styling driven directly by JS values like props or theme state, without a separate class-toggling step
Automatic scoping without any build tool involved
Guaranteed lower specificity than utility-first frameworks
mcqs.explanation: CSS-in-JS's real differentiator is expressing style rules as a function of live JS values — props, theme, state — directly inline, which BEM and CSS Modules can only approximate by toggling between pre-written classes. Classic CSS-in-JS carries real runtime cost, not zero, still typically needs build tooling, and specificity depends on implementation, not guaranteed to be lower than utility-first.

mcqs.question: How does utility-first CSS avoid the class-name collision problem that BEM only partially solves?
options: It doesn't avoid it — utility-first has the same collision risk as plain CSS
It uses runtime JS to detect and rename colliding classes automatically
There are no custom, per-component class names to collide in the first place — every class is a shared, framework-defined, single-purpose atom
It relies on a strict naming convention identical to BEM's block/element/modifier system
mcqs.explanation: Utility-first sidesteps the whole problem rather than solving it: since every class is a shared, predefined, single-purpose atom rather than a custom name someone invents per component, there's nothing project-specific to collide. It has no runtime renaming step and its scoping model is fundamentally different from BEM's convention-based approach.

mcqs.question: A team needs heavy prop-driven dynamic styling with minimal concern about runtime overhead, and already has a modern build pipeline. Which combination of traits points them toward compile-time CSS-in-JS over the classic runtime variant?
options: They want the dynamic styling capability of CSS-in-JS but without paying its classic runtime cost, which is exactly the trade-off compile-time variants make
They want zero build tooling involved in styling at all
They specifically need styles to be recalculated in the browser on every render for correctness
They want the lowest possible specificity guarantee across all styles, which only utility-first offers
mcqs.explanation: Compile-time CSS-in-JS variants exist precisely to keep the dynamic, prop-driven styling ergonomics of CSS-in-JS while extracting the actual CSS at build time instead of computing it in the browser on every render, trading some runtime flexibility for performance. It still requires build tooling, doesn't need runtime recalculation for correctness, and specificity guarantees are a separate axis from the compile-time-vs-runtime choice.
